title: How a brand kit stays alive after launch
excerpt: A brand kit stays alive when one person owns changes and the files live where the team already works. A zip file in a chat thread will fork.
alt: A person gesturing in a meeting, with a laptop showing a colorful layout, a notebook, and a phone on the table. The conversation is where a kit either gets an owner or starts to fork.
caption: Someone in the room has to own the next change. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: When should the kit change?
faqs.answer: Change it when a need repeats, such as a second screen that requires a new component. Record the decision the day it becomes shared. A campaign can have a bounded layout with an end date, and it should not rewrite the product colors for a weekend.

markdown:
Design system maintenance is the work of keeping a brand kit true after launch, when the studio is gone and the team is shipping without a critique in the room. Someone has to own changes. A short page the team can open, or a portal that holds the files, beats a zip archive lost in a chat thread.

Launch is the moment the kit is most accurate and least tested by daily use. The first new landing page, the first new hire, and the first "quick" social graphic are where it either holds or quietly forks.

## Name an owner before you celebrate the launch

The owner is the person who can accept or refuse a new color, a new type size, or a new component. On a small team that is often the founder, or the designer who is also shipping. The job is not a full-time systems role. It is a review of exceptions.

Write the owner's name on the kit page. If the name is "the team," nobody will do it. If the owner leaves, naming a successor is part of the handoff, the same as handing over the repository and the domain. A kit without an owner becomes a souvenir.

The owner's weekly work can be five minutes. Open the latest page next to the kit. Note any size, color, or component that is not in the list. Either adopt it, because the product needed it, or replace it before the next person copies it. An hour-long systems meeting is a sign the kit has become a second product.

## A page people can open, not a file they cannot find

Put the working kit where work already happens. A page in the design file with type, color, logo files, and the few components. The same values in the code the site already ships. A link in the project channel that does not rot.

A zip file fails for ordinary reasons. Someone downloads it, edits a logo for a one-off, and re-uploads a near-copy. Six weeks later there are three zips, and the newest one is not the correct one. Chat search will not save you. The file that is one click from the repo, and one click from the design tool, will.

Hanabi keeps brand files, docs, and project updates in a client portal after delivery. That is the concrete version of "a place the kit lives." Logos, tokens, and the note about what changed sit next to the project, so a new teammate does not have to ask which export is current. A portal is not required for every team. A single page with the same contents is enough when the team is five people and the files are few. The failure mode is the same either way: if the latest file is a attachment, the kit is already decaying.

## What is allowed to change

Maintenance is a set of rules for change, not a promise that nothing will change. Products grow. A new status, a new page type, or a second product will ask for something the kit does not have.

Allow a change when it is a repeated need. The second screen that requires a new component is a real signal. The first screen can keep a local solution until the repetition shows up. Record the new decision in the kit the day it becomes shared. A decision that lives only in the screen that needed it will be redrawn differently next time.

Refuse a change when it is a mood. A campaign that wants a louder palette for a week can have a bounded layout, labeled as a campaign, with an end date. It should not rewrite the product colors. The same is true of a pitch deck that restyles the interface to look more dramatic. The deck can crop and caption. It should not become the new source of truth.

Write the change down in a line: what was added, what it replaces, and who accepted it. A changelog of six lines a month is more useful than a guideline book nobody opens. The W3C's [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) are a stable reference for one class of change you should not drift on: text has to stay perceivable, and controls have to stay operable. If a new color pair fails that, the change is not ready, even if the owner likes it.

## The drift to watch in the first months

The early leaks are predictable.

- A social template made in a different tool, with type that is "close enough."
- A developer hand-tuning a spacing value to fix one card, then copying that value.
- A new illustration style for a single blog post that then becomes the house style by accident.
- Logo files exported once, then recolored in slides until the clear space rules are a memory.
- A second product, or a second site, started from a screenshot instead of from the kit.

Catch these in review, while they are single instances. A monthly pass that lists them is enough. Rebuilding the kit from scratch because "it drifted" usually means the owner was never named, and the files were never in one place.

On a Hanabi project the standard is clarity over complexity, including after launch. The kit stays small so the review stays possible. A system that requires a dedicated team to maintain is the wrong size for a company that is still one product and one site.

## When the kit should grow up

Grow the kit when a second designer, or a second product, would otherwise invent a parallel style. That growth is a project: more components, written states, and a slightly stricter review. It is still maintenance if the same person can explain every entry.

If the kit page is wrong and people are working around it, fix the page before you add process. A wrong kit that is enforced will teach the team to route around the owner. A short, accurate kit that is easy to open will be used without a policy document.

After the files have a home, the useful next question is what that home is for once the brand is delivered. That piece is [what a client portal is for](/blog/what-a-client-portal-is-for). It covers logos, tokens, docs, and updates as things a team has to find six months later, not only on launch day.
